newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-ABB below-forecast profit rise received well.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ABB below-forecast profit rise received well.

text.p: ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG on Thursday reported a smaller-than-expected rise in first-half profits as the strong dollar hid a steady improvement in the electrical engineering group's operating earnings.
"Look at the operating performance and look at the currencies, this is a strong performance," chief executive Goran Lindahl told Reuters.
ABB's group net profit in the first six months of 1997 rose two percent from last year's level to $567 million, while operating earnings rose three percent to $1.09 billion.
Although the result was below expectations for a 4.5 percent gain, most analysts shrugged off the difference.
"The results were fine. Sure a little bit below forecast but it's terribly difficult to work out what the dollar does to them," said Angela Dean of Morgan Stanley.
The stock market also gave the nod to Swiss-Swedish ABB.
After initial weakness on the results, the shares of ABB's Swiss parent company ended 2.3 percent higher at 2,266 francs.

One analyst, Thomas Pfyl of Bank Vontobel, said he had raised his earnings per share forecast for ABB and changed the rating to a "buy" from a "hold", based on an expected improvement in Western Europe in 1998.
But another analyst, Peter Gachnang of Bank Julius Baer, was disappointed with the performance.
"There is no reason to be fearful but nevertheless the result was disappointing," said Gachnang, adding that he would slightly reduce his earnings forecast.

Although ABB is owned by Swedish and Swiss parent companies, the group reports results in dollars. The strength of the dollar against European currencies tends to reduce its group results and inflate the results of its parent companies.
Expressed in local currencies, ABB's first-half group net profit rose 12 percent and operating earnings 11 percent. All ABB's business segments contributed to the higher earnings.
Lindahl said he was encouraged by the continued inflow of new orders and the growing backlog.
"In light of a better backlog, growing orders and that the business environment does not get worse, then it is encouraging for the future," Lindahl said.
New orders to ABB in the first half rose 14 percent to $20 billion -- pushing the order backlog up to $35.3 billion -- on strong growth in large projects and increased demand from emerging markets.
"This is a very good growth rate and show the efforts to penetrate markets, especially the emerging markets, is giving good rewards," Lindahl said.
ABB also confirmed its forecast for 1997 net profit to at least reach 1996's $1.233 billion, a forecast that Lindahl has described as setting a minimum for what profits could be.
Analysts on average forecast a 5.0 percent increase in ABB's 1997 net profit to $1.295 billion.
All ABB's segments contributed to the better operating peformance with the strongest regional growth coming from Poland and Britain.
Profits from the U.S. market also continued to improve and results from Latin America were substantiall higher than last year. Earnings from the Asian-Pacific region were unchanged.
ABB's worldwide workforce grew to 216,000 from 215,000, mainly due to new ventures and acquisitions.
